title: Bedtime Stories for Adults 🌙 Night Shifts and Quiet Streets | Snortlo
intro: Hello, and welcome. This is Snortlo, and tonight I have six gentle stories for you, about night shifts, quiet streets, and small warm places. Before we begin, let yourself get settled. Dim the lights, or turn them off altogether. Pull the blanket up a little, and let your shoulders drop. You don't need to stay awake until the end. If you drift off halfway through, that is exactly right. The stories will keep going quietly without you. Let's take one slow breath together. In, and out. Good. Let's begin.

stories.title: The Greenhouse on a Frosty Night
stories.text:
At the very end of Ruth's long, narrow garden, past the apple tree and the bench that wobbled, there was a small glass greenhouse. It had a green painted door that stuck a little in damp weather, and a latch that went clack when you lifted it. Ruth had kept it for thirty years. In the summer it smelled of tomato leaves and warm soil. In the autumn it smelled of earth and rain and something sweet that she could never quite name.

On this particular evening, the radio in the kitchen said there would be a frost. The first proper frost of the year. The man on the radio said it in a calm voice, the way people say things they have said every autumn for a long time. Ruth turned the radio off, dried the last teacup, and looked out of the window at the sky. It was very clear. The stars were coming out one at a time, like someone was switching them on by hand.

She put on her thick grey cardigan, the one with the wooden buttons, and then her wool hat with the bobble on top. She filled a flask with hot tea and a spoonful of honey. She took the old lantern from its hook by the back door, lit it, and stepped out into the garden.

The air was cold and very still. The grass was already stiff under her slippers, and her breath made little clouds that drifted up and vanished. The apple tree stood quietly with its last few leaves. A blackbird gave one small, sleepy chirp from somewhere in the hedge, and then said nothing more.

Ruth lifted the latch. Clack. The green door stuck, as it always did, and then gave way with a soft sigh. Inside, the greenhouse was dark and a little warmer than the garden. She hung the lantern from the hook in the roof, and the glass walls filled with a gentle golden glow. Her own reflection looked back at her from every side, a small woman in a bobble hat, surrounded by plants.

"Good evening, everyone," she said. "There's a frost coming. But don't you worry. We've done this before."

First she lit the little stove in the corner. It was an old iron thing with a round window in its door, and when the flame caught, it made a quiet ticking sound as the metal warmed. Tick, tick, tick. A soft orange light flickered through the round window and danced on the floor.

Then she began her rounds.

Along the left side were the geraniums, standing in their clay pots like a row of patient old friends. They were red and pink and one was a pale salmon colour that Ruth was secretly the most fond of. She touched each one lightly on the leaves.

"You've been very good this year," she told them. "Lots of flowers. Nobody could ask for more."

She lifted a folded sheet of soft white fleece from the shelf and draped it over the geraniums, tucking the edges under the pots, the way you might tuck a blanket around someone who has fallen asleep on the sofa.

Next came the lemon tree. It was only as tall as Ruth's shoulder, and it lived in a big blue pot on wheels so she could roll it in and out with the seasons. It had three small green lemons on it, and one that was just beginning to turn yellow. Ruth leaned close and breathed in. Even the leaves smelled of lemon.

"Now you," she said, "are a long way from home. I know you don't care for the cold. So you can sit right here next to the stove, and you'll be as warm as toast."

She rolled the blue pot slowly across the floor. The little wheels squeaked. She settled it near the stove, not too close, and wrapped a piece of fleece loosely around its trunk like a scarf.

Along the back wall were trays of seedlings. These were for next spring. Sweet peas and tiny lettuces and a row of something she had planted and forgotten to label. They were very small, with only two or three leaves each, and they leaned towards the lantern light as if they were curious about it.

"You're the babies," Ruth said, and her voice went softer without her trying. "You just keep still and sleep. That's all you have to do tonight."

She laid a sheet of newspaper over each tray, very gently, so that it rested on the edges and didn't touch the leaves. The paper rustled. Then it was still.

In the far corner, hanging from the roof in a basket, was the spider plant. It was the oldest thing in the greenhouse. It had been a gift, many years ago, and it had grown so many little baby plants on long trailing stems that it looked like a green waterfall. Ruth reached up and turned the basket a quarter turn, so a different side would face the stove.

"And you," she said, "have seen more frosts than I can count. You can tell the others it's nothing to fuss about."

The spider plant swayed very slightly, and Ruth decided that this meant yes.

When the rounds were done, she sat down in the wicker chair by the door. It creaked as it took her weight, the same creak it had made for years. She unscrewed the lid of the flask, and steam curled up into the lantern light. She poured the tea into the lid, which was also a cup, and held it in both hands to warm them.

Outside, the frost was beginning. She could see it happening, if she watched very closely. On the outside of the glass, tiny feathers of white were growing from the corners of each pane. They spread slowly, branching and curling, like ferns drawn with the finest silver pen. The lawn beyond had turned pale under the moon. The bench that wobbled was white on top. The apple tree glittered at the tips of its twigs.

Inside, it was warm and smelled of soil and lemon leaves and the faint, homely smell of the stove. The flame ticked. The fleece over the geraniums rose and fell a tiny bit in the warm air, as if they were breathing.

Ruth sipped her tea. It was sweet with the honey and very hot, and it warmed her all the way down.

She thought about the summer, when the tomatoes had grown so tall they touched the roof, and about the spring that was coming, when the seedlings would be big enough to plant out. She thought about how many frosty nights she had sat in this very chair, and how each one felt a little bit the same and a little bit new.

After a while her eyes began to feel heavy. The tea was finished. The stove had settled into a low, steady glow.

Ruth stood up slowly, and the wicker chair creaked goodbye. She checked the stove one last time and turned it down to its smallest flame, just enough to keep the chill away until morning. She looked around at all her sleeping plants under their blankets and papers.

"Goodnight, everyone," she said. "I'll see you in the morning."

She took the lantern from its hook, stepped out, and pulled the green door closed behind her. It stuck, and then it shut. Clack.

The grass crunched softly under her slippers as she walked back up the long garden. Behind her, the greenhouse glowed faintly orange through the frosted glass, like a small lamp left on in a window.

In the kitchen, she hung up the lantern and put the flask by the sink. She looked out once more at the little orange glow at the end of the garden.

Then she turned off the kitchen light, and went upstairs to bed.

And at the bottom of the garden, the stove ticked quietly through the night. Tick. Tick. Tick.

stories.title: The Clock Shop at Closing
stories.text:
On a narrow street near the middle of town, between a bakery that had already closed for the night and a shop that sold buttons and thread, there was a little clock shop. The sign above the window was painted in gold letters that had faded to the colour of honey. Inside, every wall was covered in clocks.

There were tall clocks standing in the corners like quiet guards. There were round clocks with plain white faces, and square clocks with painted flowers, and one clock shaped like a small wooden house with a bird that lived inside it. There were brass carriage clocks on the shelves and pocket watches lying in a glass case, their chains coiled like sleeping snakes. And all of them, every single one, were ticking.

The man who owned the shop was called Walt. He had owned it for forty years, and before that it had belonged to his father. Walt was tall and a little stooped, with silver hair that stuck up at the back no matter how often he smoothed it down. He wore a brown apron with deep pockets, and in the pockets he kept tiny screwdrivers, a little brush, a magnifying glass, and usually a peppermint.

It was evening now, and the street outside was quiet. A light rain had been falling since teatime, soft and fine, and the window was speckled with drops that caught the glow of the street lamp. Walt turned the sign on the door from open to closed. He switched off the big overhead light, leaving just the green lamp on his workbench and the small lamps glowing here and there between the clocks.

Then he did what he did every evening, at the end of every day.

He began to set the clocks.

You see, clocks are a little like people. Left alone, they drift. One runs a minute fast. Another runs two minutes slow. The tall clock in the corner liked to lose a little time every afternoon, as if it was having a rest. The cuckoo clock was always in a hurry. By the end of each day, they were all saying slightly different things, like a room full of friends who have each told the same story in their own way.

So every evening, Walt walked slowly around the shop and brought them all back together.

He started with the tall clock by the door. It was made of dark wood, almost black, and its pendulum swung behind a little glass window, back and forth, back and forth, with a deep and patient tock. Walt opened the glass door in its face, and with one finger he moved the long hand forward, just a touch.

"There you are," he said. "You were dreaming again."

He closed the little door. Tock, went the clock, as if to say thank you.

Next were the round clocks on the left wall. There were eleven of them, in a neat row, and Walt checked each one against the old silver pocket watch he kept on a chain at his waist. The watch had been his father's. It was the most reliable thing in the shop, and maybe in the whole town. Walt adjusted one clock, then the next, then skipped one that was already right, and gave it a little nod of approval.

The carriage clocks on the shelf needed winding. Each had a small brass key, and Walt turned each key slowly, counting the turns under his breath. Click, click, click, click. Not too tight. Never too tight. A clock should be wound like you are tucking it in, he always said, not like you are tightening a bolt.

The little wooden house with the bird inside was last. It was the cuckoo clock, painted with tiny leaves and a tiny red door, and it was always, always fast. Walt gently moved its hands back by three whole minutes.

"You're always in such a rush," he told it. "There's nowhere to be. It's raining. Everyone's at home."

The cuckoo clock said nothing, because it was not yet time.

When all the clocks were set, Walt went back to his workbench and sat down on his tall wooden stool. On the bench was the clock he had been mending that afternoon. It belonged to a lady from the edge of town, and it was small and round with a blue enamel face and a little picture of a sailing boat painted on it. It had stopped one morning, quite suddenly, and she had brought it in wrapped in a tea towel, the way you might carry a sleeping kitten.

Walt had found the problem. A tiny spring, no bigger than an eyelash, had slipped out of place. He bent over the clock now with his magnifying glass in one eye, and with the smallest screwdriver he nudged the spring back where it belonged. He breathed out very slowly while he did it, the way he always did when the work was delicate.

Then he gave the clock a gentle wind, and set it down, and waited.

Tick.

Tick. Tick. Tick.

Walt smiled. He set its hands to match his father's watch, and placed it on the shelf beside the others. It would go home tomorrow, wrapped in its tea towel.

He took the peppermint from his apron pocket, unwrapped it, and put it in his mouth. The paper crinkled. Outside, the rain was still falling, fine and soft. A car passed slowly, its tyres hissing on the wet road, and its headlights swept across the ceiling and were gone.

Now came the part of the day that Walt loved best.

He looked at his father's watch. It was nearly nine o'clock. Less than a minute to go. He put both hands flat on the workbench, and he listened.

The whole shop was ticking. Dozens and dozens of clocks, big and small, all ticking together. Usually the ticks were a jumble, like rain on a roof, each one in its own time. But tonight, because Walt had set them so carefully, many of them had fallen into step. The sound had become something like a slow, steady heartbeat, filling the room.

The second hands swept upward together. The minute hands crept towards the top.

And then, all at once, every clock in the shop struck nine.

The tall clock by the door went first, with a deep, round bong that you could feel in the floorboards. Then the round clocks joined in with their bright little chimes. The carriage clocks rang like tiny silver bells. Somewhere a clock played a short tune, four notes going up and four notes coming down. And the little wooden house threw open its red door, and the bird popped out and called, cuckoo, cuckoo, cuckoo, nine times, perfectly on time for once.

For a few seconds, the shop was full of sound, warm and shimmering, like being inside a music box.

Then, one by one, the chimes faded. The last bong of the tall clock hummed for a long moment in the air and slowly, slowly disappeared. The bird went back inside its little house, and the red door clicked shut.

And the ticking went on, soft and steady, as if nothing had happened at all.

Walt sat for a moment with his eyes closed, just listening. It happened only once a day, and only because he made it happen. Nobody else in town ever heard it. He liked it that way. It was his small secret, a little gift he gave to the shop, and that the shop gave back to him.

He opened his eyes. He hung up his apron on its peg by the back door. He switched off the green lamp on the workbench, and then the small lamps, one by one, until only the glow from the street lamp came in through the rainy window and lay in soft gold squares on the floor.

He put on his coat, and his hat, and took his umbrella from the stand.

"Goodnight," he said to the clocks.

He stepped out into the rain and locked the door behind him. The umbrella opened with a soft whump. He walked slowly down the wet street, his footsteps quiet on the stones.

And behind him, in the dark little shop, the clocks went on ticking together, keeping time for the whole sleeping town.

stories.title: The Postman's Dog
stories.text:
Henry had been the village postman for thirty one years. He had walked every lane and every path, up every garden and back again, in sunshine and snow and the kind of sideways rain that gets into your sleeves. He knew which gates squeaked and which dogs barked and which houses had a cup of tea waiting on the step on cold mornings.

Then, one spring, he retired. And for about a week, he did not know what to do with his legs.

That was when Biscuit arrived.

Biscuit was a dog of no particular kind. She was medium sized and sandy coloured, with one ear that stood up and one ear that flopped over, and a tail that went round in circles when she was pleased. She had come from a farm on the hill where there had been a few too many puppies, and she had looked at Henry in a way that said, quite clearly, I think you need me.

She was right. And from the very first evening, it was Biscuit who decided where they would walk.

This evening was a cool one, in the middle of autumn. The sun had gone down behind the hill, and the sky was turning from orange to lavender to a deep, soft blue. Henry put on his old navy jacket, the one with the elbow patches, and wound a scarf twice around his neck. He took the lead from its hook by the door. Biscuit was already sitting on the doormat, her tail sweeping the floor, swish, swish, swish.

"Well then," said Henry. "Where are we going tonight?"

Biscuit did not answer. But the moment the door opened, she trotted down the path and turned left, which meant they were going the long way round.

The lane was quiet. The houses had their curtains half drawn, and lamps were coming on behind them, one here, one there, little squares of yellow light. Somewhere someone was cooking onions, and the smell drifted over a hedge and followed them for a while. Leaves lay in heaps along the edge of the road, brown and gold and rust, and Biscuit walked straight through every heap she could find. Crunch, crunch, crunch.

At the first corner was the house with the blue door. When Henry was the postman, the lady who lived there had always left a biscuit on the windowsill for him. Not a dog biscuit. A proper one, with chocolate. She still did, sometimes, even now. Biscuit stopped at the gate and sat down very straight and very politely, and looked at the window.

"No," said Henry. "That was for me, not for you. And it was years ago."

But the curtain moved, and the window opened, and a hand came out holding a small, plain dog treat. "Evening, Henry," said a voice. "Evening, Biscuit."

"Evening, Mrs. Lowe," said Henry. "You spoil her."

"Somebody has to," said Mrs. Lowe, and the window closed.

Biscuit ate her treat in one bite and trotted on, looking very pleased with herself.

Next she led him down the little path between the church wall and the field, where the grass was long and wet with evening dew. There were sheep in the field, pale shapes in the dusk, and one of them lifted its head and said baa in a low, sleepy voice. Biscuit stopped and looked at the sheep. The sheep looked at Biscuit. Neither of them seemed to think much of the other, and after a moment, they both went back to what they were doing.

The path came out by the stream. This was Biscuit's favourite part. The water ran quick and shallow over smooth brown stones, and it made a soft, chattering sound, like a crowd of people whispering far away. There was a little wooden bridge with a handrail worn smooth by years of hands. Henry stopped in the middle of the bridge, as he always did, and leaned on the rail. Biscuit sat beside his feet and watched the water.

Henry remembered crossing this bridge with his postbag on his shoulder, hundreds of times, thousands of times. He remembered the letters he had carried. Birthday cards with stiff envelopes. Postcards from the seaside. Parcels that rattled and parcels that didn't. A letter that a young man had written to the girl at the farm, and then, a year later, a big cream envelope with their wedding invitation inside, and Henry had been invited too.

He had carried a lot of the village's news, over the years. Now he just carried a lead and a pocketful of treats. But he found he didn't mind. The bridge was the same. The stream was the same. The evening was just as lovely.

Biscuit stood up and stretched, front legs first and then back legs, and gave a big yawn that ended in a squeak. Time to go.

She did not take him home, though. Not yet. She led him up the hill, past the old post office, which was a little café now with chairs stacked on the tables inside. She led him past the school, which was dark and empty, with paintings of autumn trees stuck on the windows. She led him past the bus shelter, where a cat was sitting on the bench, very upright, as if waiting for a bus that would never come. Biscuit pretended not to see the cat. The cat pretended not to see Biscuit. It was an arrangement that worked for everyone.

At the top of the hill, there was a bench under a big old chestnut tree. From the bench, you could see the whole village laid out below, the rooftops and chimneys and the church tower, and all the little lights in all the little windows.

Biscuit sat down beside the bench and looked at Henry until he sat down too.

So he did. The bench was cold and a little damp, but his jacket was warm. The sky was almost fully dark now, and the first stars had come out over the hill. A chimney somewhere was puffing out wood smoke, and the smell of it drifted up, sweet and cosy.

Henry looked down at the village, at all those lit windows, and he knew who lived behind nearly every one. There was the baker's house, where the light was already off because the baker went to bed early. There was the farmhouse, where the young couple from the wedding invitation now lived with two small children and a very large ginger cat. There was Mrs. Lowe's blue door. There was his own little house, at the end of the lane, dark and waiting.

Biscuit put her chin on his knee. Her ear that stood up stood up. Her ear that flopped flopped. Her tail went round, slowly, once.

"You know," said Henry, "I used to think I knew every way round this village. But you've shown me a few I never tried."

Biscuit closed her eyes, as if to say, I know.

They sat there for a while, the old postman and his sandy dog, while the stars came out one by one and the village grew quiet beneath them. An owl hooted from the chestnut tree, once, and then again. Somewhere far off, a door closed.

At last, Biscuit stood up and shook herself, ears flapping, and set off down the hill. Henry followed. She took them home the short way this time, straight down the lane, past the hedges and the gates and the heaps of leaves.

At their own front door, she sat down on the mat and waited while Henry found his key.

Inside, the house was cool and dark. Henry switched on the lamp by the window. He filled Biscuit's water bowl, and she drank noisily, lap, lap, lap. He made himself a cup of cocoa and sat down in his armchair. Biscuit climbed into her basket by the radiator, turned around three times, and settled with a long, contented sigh.

"Same time tomorrow," said Henry.

Biscuit's tail thumped once against the side of the basket.

Henry drank his cocoa slowly, and the lamp glowed softly in the window, and outside, the village went to sleep.

stories.title: The Night Porter
stories.text:
The hotel stood on the corner of a quiet square, in the old part of the city. It was not a big hotel. It had four floors, a revolving door that turned with a soft whoosh, and a lobby with a black and white tiled floor and a large green plant in a brass pot. There were twenty two rooms, and a bell on the front desk that went ting when you pressed it.

Theo was the night porter. He started work at ten in the evening, when the day staff went home, and he finished at six in the morning, when the cook arrived to start the breakfast. In between, the hotel belonged to him.

He liked it best of all just after midnight. That was when the last guests had come in from the theatre or from dinner, shaking the cold off their coats, and had taken their keys and gone up in the little lift. The lift went up with a hum and a clunk, and then the hotel became very still.

Tonight it was snowing. Not heavily, just a slow, soft snow that drifted down past the tall windows of the lobby and settled on the railings of the square outside. The street lamps wore little white caps. The fountain in the middle of the square had been turned off for the winter, and its stone basin was slowly filling with white.

Theo made himself a cup of tea in the tiny kitchen behind the front desk. He used the blue mug that was his, the one with the chip on the handle. He stirred in one sugar, chink, chink, chink, and carried it back to the desk. He sat on the tall stool and looked out at the snow, and he listened to the hotel.

Every building has its night sounds, and Theo knew all of this one's. The radiators made a soft knocking now and then, like someone tapping politely on a door. The big clock above the stairs ticked in a slow, important way. The lift sometimes gave a small sigh all on its own, as if it was dreaming of going up and down. And very faintly, from somewhere on the second floor, came the sound of someone snoring, gentle and steady, like waves on a beach.

When his tea was finished, Theo began his rounds.

First, the brass. There was a great deal of brass in the hotel. There was the brass rail that ran along the front desk, and the brass handles on the revolving door, and the brass numbers on the doors upstairs. There was the brass pot that the big plant lived in, and the brass bell, and the brass plate by the lift that said, in curly letters, please ring for assistance.

Theo kept a soft yellow cloth and a little tin of polish in the drawer under the desk. He started with the rail. He rubbed a small dab of polish onto the cloth and worked it in slow circles along the brass, and the dull metal underneath slowly began to shine, warm and golden, until he could see his own face in it, a little stretched and wobbly.

He moved on to the door handles. Then the bell. He polished the bell so carefully that when he finished, he pressed it once, very softly, just to hear it. Ting. The sound floated up the stairwell and faded away.

Next he walked the corridors. He went up the stairs rather than taking the lift, because the lift was noisy and the guests were sleeping. The carpet on the stairs was deep red and very soft, and his footsteps made no sound at all. On each floor, he walked slowly from one end of the corridor to the other. He straightened a painting of a sailing ship that had gone a little crooked. He picked up a newspaper that someone had left outside their door and folded it neatly on the little table by the window. He checked that the window at the end of the third floor corridor was closed, because it liked to creep open on windy nights.

Outside the window, the snow was still falling. The square below was completely white now, smooth and untouched, with the lamps glowing softly in the falling flakes.

When he came back down to the lobby, the lift was waiting with its door open, and a man was standing beside the front desk.

He was a guest from the fourth floor. He was wearing striped pyjamas and the white hotel dressing gown and a pair of hotel slippers that were slightly too small for him. His hair was flat on one side, the way hair is when it has been on a pillow. He looked very sleepy and a little embarrassed.

"Hello," said the man. "I'm so sorry. I've forgotten my toothbrush. I only noticed just now. I've been lying there thinking about it for an hour."

Theo smiled. In twelve years of night shifts, he had learned that the most common thing in the world, after midnight, was a forgotten toothbrush.

"That's no trouble at all," he said. "Just one moment."

He went to the cupboard behind the desk. It was a tall wooden cupboard with many small drawers, and Theo knew exactly what was in every one. There were sewing kits and spare buttons, combs and shoe polish, plasters and phone chargers and three spare umbrellas. There was a drawer just for socks, because people forgot socks more often than you would think. And there was a drawer full of toothbrushes, each one in its own little paper sleeve, next to a row of tiny tubes of toothpaste.

Theo took one of each and put them on the desk.

"There you are," he said. "And would you like anything else, while you're down? A glass of warm milk, perhaps? It helps, I find."

The man looked surprised, and then very grateful. "Do you know," he said, "I think I would."

So Theo went to the little kitchen and warmed some milk in a small pan on the stove. He watched it carefully, so that it would not boil, and when tiny bubbles appeared around the edge, he poured it into a white cup and added a little spoonful of honey. He put the cup on a saucer, with a plain biscuit on the side.

The man sat in one of the big leather armchairs by the window, in his dressing gown and his too small slippers, and drank his milk, and watched the snow falling in the square.

"It's very peaceful down here," he said.

"It is," said Theo. "This is the best time. Everyone's safe inside, and the snow is doing all the work."

The man laughed softly. He finished his milk, and the biscuit, and stood up, and thanked Theo three times. Then he took his toothbrush and his toothpaste and went back to the lift. The doors closed with a hum, and Theo heard it go up, slowly, all the way to the fourth floor, and stop with a gentle clunk.

He washed the cup and the pan and the saucer, dried them, and put them away.

Then he went back to his stool behind the shining brass rail and sat down. The radiators knocked softly. The big clock ticked. The lift sighed, all on its own. From the second floor, the gentle snoring went on, like waves on a beach.

Outside, the snow kept falling, covering the square in a deeper and deeper layer of white. Soon it would be morning, and the cook would arrive, stamping her boots on the mat, and the hotel would wake up and fill with the smell of coffee and toast. But that was still a long way off.

For now, everything was quiet. Everyone was sleeping. And Theo, the night porter, sat in the warm lamplight of the lobby, watching over all of them while the snow came softly down.

stories.title: The Hut on the Mountain
stories.text:
High up on the side of a mountain, above the last of the pine trees, where the path turned from earth to stone, there was a small wooden hut. It had a steep roof to let the snow slide off, a chimney made of grey stones, and a single round window that looked down the valley. A wooden sign by the door said, in plain carved letters, the hut is open, come in and get warm.

The warden of the hut was called June. She lived there from the end of spring to the start of winter, and her job was simple. She kept the hut clean. She kept the beds made. And above all, she kept the stove lit, so that anyone who came up the path, at any hour, would find a warm room waiting.

This evening, it had been raining since lunchtime. Not a storm, just a long, steady, grey kind of rain that had settled over the mountain like a blanket and decided to stay. It pattered on the roof. It ran in little streams from the edges of the eaves. It made the stones on the path dark and shiny, and it filled the valley below with soft white cloud.

June didn't mind the rain. She liked the sound of it on the roof. It made the inside of the hut feel even cosier.

She knelt by the stove and opened its heavy iron door. Inside, the fire had burned down to a bed of glowing orange coals. She chose two logs from the basket, pine logs that she had split herself in the summer, and laid them carefully on top. For a moment, nothing happened. Then a little flame curled up around the edge of one log, and then another, and soon the fire was crackling and popping cheerfully. June closed the door, and the stove began to tick and hum as it heated up.

The hut had one main room. Along one wall was a long wooden table with benches on either side. Along the other wall were bunk beds, six of them, each with a folded grey blanket and a pillow at the end. Above the stove there was a rack made of wooden poles, for drying wet clothes. And in the corner, on a small shelf, there was a row of books that hikers had left behind over the years, and a jar of pencils, and an old guestbook with a cloth cover.

Nobody had come up the path today. June had thought perhaps nobody would, in this rain. But she had a feeling, the kind of feeling you get after many summers on a mountain, that someone was still on their way.

So she put a big pot on top of the stove, and began to make soup.

She chopped onions and carrots and potatoes on the wooden board, chop, chop, chop, and dropped them into the pot. She added a handful of dried herbs from a paper bag, and a spoonful of salt, and a jug of water from the barrel that collected rain from the roof. Soon the pot began to bubble softly, and the whole hut filled with a warm, savoury smell.

Outside, the light was fading. The cloud in the valley turned from white to grey to a soft blue. June lit the lantern and hung it in the round window, the way she always did at dusk. From down the path, the little window would glow like a small yellow moon.

Then she sat at the table with a cup of tea and a book, and waited.

She had read nearly three chapters when she heard it. Footsteps on the stones outside. Slow and tired footsteps, and voices, low and cheerful. Then a knock at the door.

June opened it. Standing in the rain were two hikers, a young man and a young woman, with big packs on their backs and hoods pulled down low. They were wet from head to toe. Water was dripping off the ends of their noses. The young man's boots squelched when he shifted his weight.

"Hello," said the young woman. "We saw your light. Is there room?"

"There's always room," said June. "Come in, come in. Boots off by the door."

The hikers came in, bringing a gust of cold, wet air with them, and June closed the door behind them. They stood dripping on the mat and looked around at the warm room, the glowing stove, the bubbling pot, and both of their faces broke into the same tired smile.

"Oh," said the young man. "Oh, that's lovely."

Their names were Nora and Sam. They had been walking all day, they said, and had planned to reach the hut by teatime. But the rain had made the path slow, and they had stopped to watch a family of goats on a ledge, and then they had taken a wrong turn by a big rock and had to come back. They had been very glad to see the yellow light in the window.

"Everyone takes the wrong turn by the big rock," said June. "I keep meaning to paint an arrow on it."

She showed them where to hang their wet jackets on the rack above the stove. Soon the jackets were steaming gently in the heat. Their socks went up next, side by side, and then two pairs of gloves, and a hat with a bobble. June gave them each a pair of thick wool socks from the box of spares, and they pulled them on and wiggled their toes and sighed.

Then she ladled soup into three bowls and cut thick slices from a loaf of brown bread, and they all sat down together at the long wooden table.

For a while, nobody said anything at all. There was only the sound of spoons on bowls, and the crackle of the fire, and the rain pattering on the roof. The soup was hot and thick, and the bread was soft, and the hikers ate two bowls each and then a third.

"This is the best soup I have ever had," said Sam, very seriously.

"That's the mountain," said June. "Everything tastes better after a long walk up."

After supper, they sat by the stove. Nora found a book on the shelf, a slim book about mountain flowers with little drawings in it, and turned the pages slowly. Sam wrote in the guestbook with one of the pencils from the jar. He wrote the date, and their names, and then, after a moment's thought, he wrote, thank you for the light in the window.

June read it later, after they had gone to bed. It was her favourite kind of entry. There were quite a lot like it, over the years.

The hikers climbed into the bunk beds and pulled the grey blankets up to their chins. Within a few minutes, they were both asleep. Nora breathed slow and deep. Sam made a tiny whistling sound through his nose, very soft.

June moved quietly around the room. She turned the jackets on the rack so the other side would dry. She added one more log to the stove, a big one, so that it would burn slowly through the night. She washed the bowls in the basin and set them upside down on the shelf. She closed the guestbook and put it back in its place.

Then she sat down in her own chair by the stove, the old wooden one with a cushion on the seat, and pulled a blanket over her knees.

Outside, the rain had softened. It was barely more than a whisper on the roof now. Through the round window, past the glow of the lantern, she could see that the cloud in the valley was thinning, and here and there, between the drifting grey, a few stars were shining.

The fire crackled. The stove ticked. The wet jackets dripped, now and then, onto the warm stone floor, plip, and then a long while later, plip.

June looked at the two sleeping hikers, and the warm stove, and the lantern glowing in the window. She thought about all the people who had come up that path over all the years, tired and wet and glad, and all the bowls of soup, and all the socks hung up to dry.

She left the lantern burning in the window, just in case.

Then she closed her eyes, and listened to the soft rain on the roof, and slept.

stories.title: The Last Warm Day
stories.text:
At the far end of the promenade, where the paving stones gave way to sand and the beach huts stood in a row like a box of coloured crayons, there was a little ice cream kiosk. It was painted pale mint green, with a striped awning in pink and white, and a hatch in the front that folded up in the morning and folded down at night. Above the hatch, a hand painted sign said, ices, cones and wafers, made fresh.

The kiosk belonged to Mabel. She had run it for twenty five summers. She opened it every year on the first warm day of spring, and she closed it every year on the last warm day of autumn. And today, though nobody had said so out loud, everyone could feel that it was the last warm day.

The sun had shone all afternoon, low and golden, in a way that it only does at the end of the season. The sea had been calm and blue and full of glitter. People had come down to the beach in their coats but then taken them off, surprised, and sat on the sand with their sleeves rolled up. Children had built one last sandcastle. Dogs had chased one last ball into the waves. And nearly everyone, at some point in the afternoon, had wandered along the promenade to Mabel's kiosk for one last ice cream.

Now it was evening. The sun was sinking towards the edge of the sea, turning the whole sky peach and rose and gold. The beach was nearly empty. The tide was coming in slowly, with a long, soft hush, and each wave left a thin line of foam on the sand before it slid back again.

Mabel leaned on the counter of her hatch and watched the last few people heading home. A family with a pushchair and a bucket full of shells. An old man walking very slowly with an even older dog. A boy on a bicycle, ringing his bell twice as he passed, ding ding, and waving.

"Same time next year, Mabel," he called.

"Same time next year," she called back.

Then she began to close up.

First, the freezer. Inside the kiosk, under the counter, was a long glass freezer with eight metal tubs of ice cream in a row. There was vanilla, which was the most popular, and strawberry, which was the prettiest, and chocolate, which was the most reliable. There was a mint one with little flecks of chocolate in it, and a honey one made with honey from a farm up the coast. There was a toffee one, and a lemon sorbet, and one tub of a pale green flavour that Mabel had invented this summer and called sea breeze, which tasted of apple and cucumber and was much more delicious than it sounds.

She looked into each tub. Most were nearly empty. She scraped what was left of the vanilla into a little paper cup for herself, and then she lifted the tubs out one by one and carried them to the sink at the back.

She washed the tubs in warm, soapy water. She washed the scoops, the big round one and the small round one and the flat paddle she used for sorbet. She washed the jug where the scoops stood between customers. The water was warm and smelled of lemon soap, and the bubbles caught the light from the window and shone pink and gold.

Next, the cones. There was a tall stack of them still, in their paper sleeves, and a half full tin of the little flat wafers that went into the side of the ice cream like a sail. Mabel wrapped them all carefully and packed them into a cardboard box, and wrote on the lid in pencil, cones, for next year. She tucked the box onto the top shelf.

Then she wiped every surface. The counter, the shelves, the glass of the freezer, the little ledge where people put their elbows while they decided. She wiped the jar where she kept the paper napkins, and the jar where she kept the wooden spoons, and the small brass bell that people rang when she was round the back.

When everything was clean, she sat on her little folding stool in the open hatch with her paper cup of vanilla, and she watched the sun go down.

It was a very good sunset. The sun was a great orange circle now, just touching the sea, and it laid a long path of light across the water, right up to the beach, as if you could walk along it all the way to the horizon. A few seagulls drifted past, high and slow, their wings glowing on the underside. Out on the water, a small fishing boat was heading home, its little engine putting along, put put put put, so far away it was almost a sound you were imagining.

Mabel ate her vanilla with the small wooden spoon. It was soft at the edges, the way ice cream gets at the end of the day, and it was very good.

She thought about the summer. The hot days in July when the queue had stretched past three beach huts. The rainy day in August when nobody came at all, and she had sat in the kiosk reading a whole book. The little girl who had dropped her cone on the sand and cried, and how Mabel had given her a new one with two scoops, and how the little girl had come back every Saturday after that to say hello. The man who had ordered sea breeze as a joke, and then come back for it four days in a row.

Twenty five summers. Each one a little bit the same and a little bit different.

The sun slipped down into the sea. For a moment the whole sky held its colour, warm and glowing, and then slowly it began to fade, peach to lilac to a deep and gentle blue. The first star came out, just above the end of the pier. The street lamps along the promenade flickered on, one after another, all the way back towards the town.

The air was turning cool now. Mabel could feel it on her arms. Summer was over. She didn't feel sad about it, not really. She felt the way you feel at the end of a long, happy day, tired and full and ready for a rest.

She finished the last of her vanilla and dropped the cup and the spoon into the bin.

Then she stood up and folded her stool, and leaned it against the wall. She reached up and unhooked the striped awning, and it rolled up with a soft flap, flap. She took hold of the hatch and lowered it slowly, slowly, until it closed with a gentle clunk, and the inside of the kiosk was dark except for the thin line of lamplight under the door.

She locked the hatch from the inside, and stepped out of the little side door, and locked that too. She gave the mint green wall a pat with her hand, the way you might pat a good horse at the end of a long ride.

"Well done," she said. "Rest now. I'll see you in the spring."

She tucked her keys in her pocket and walked slowly back along the promenade towards the town. On her left, the beach huts stood in their row, all closed up for the winter. On her right, the sea was dark now, and quiet, with just a faint shimmer of silver where the moon was rising.

The tide came in, and went out, and came in again. Hush. And hush. And hush.

And at the far end of the promenade, the little mint green kiosk sat quietly under the stars, dreaming of summer, and waiting for the first warm day of spring.

outro: And that is the end of tonight's stories. Let everything grow quiet now. The little stove is ticking in the frosty greenhouse, and the clocks are keeping time for the sleeping town. Biscuit is curled in her basket by the radiator, the snow is falling softly on the hotel square, the lantern glows in the mountain window, and the mint green kiosk is resting by the sea. There are more stories waiting on the channel whenever you need them. Goodnight. Sleep well.
description:
Six cozy, original bedtime stories for grown-ups, read slowly to help you unwind and drift off.
A greenhouse on a frosty night, a clock shop at closing time, a retired postman and his dog, a hotel night porter in the snow, a mountain hut in the rain, and a seaside ice cream kiosk on the last warm day.
No cliffhangers, no drama. Just quiet places and kind people.
Goodnight 🌙
